turns.doctor_question: Hi, welcome in—I'm Dr. [Name]. What brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Hi, doctor. Well, honestly, I'm here because... ever since those foreclosure notices started coming, I just feel like I’m coming apart at the seams. 

It's affecting everything. I'm sitting out there crying in my truck before work, and I jump every single time the phone rings. And at work—I'm a heavy equipment mechanic—I'm snapping at the apprentices and making these stupid mistakes in the repair bay that I never, ever would’ve made before. I just can't seem to keep it together right now.

symptom_reasoning.S081: The patient describes acute emotional and behavioral distress (crying, hyper-reactivity, irritability, and uncharacteristic work mistakes) developing directly in response to an identifiable stressor (foreclosure notices).

turns.doctor_question: When did you first receive the foreclosure notices, and about how long after that did you start noticing these crying spells and being on edge?
turns.patient_response:
Honestly, I was functioning completely normally before all this. The first formal notice showed up in the mail... maybe a couple months ago? The phone calls started right around then, too. 

It really didn't take long for things to go downhill after that. I'd say within just a few weeks of getting that first letter, my whole life—at work and at home—just started unraveling.

symptom_reasoning.S081: The patient confirms that their life began unraveling within a few weeks of receiving foreclosure notices, demonstrating emotional and behavioral symptoms arising directly in response to an identifiable stressor.

turns.doctor_question: Besides the crying and feeling on edge, have you noticed a persistent low or sad mood most of the day, or a loss of interest or pleasure in things you used to enjoy, over these past couple of months?
turns.patient_response: No, not really. I mean, I'm stressed and I'm a wreck about the house, but I don't feel sad all day long. And it's not like I don't want to do things I used to enjoy... I just can't focus on them right now because I'm so worried about losing my home.

symptom_reasoning.S024: The patient explicitly states that they do not feel sad all day long in response to the inquiry about persistent low mood.
symptom_reasoning.S025: The patient denies losing interest in activities, clarifying that they still want to do things they enjoy but are distracted by worry.

turns.doctor_question: Is your worrying mostly about the foreclosure and your finances, or do you find yourself excessively worrying about a lot of other things in your life too, like your health, family, or work in general?
turns.patient_response: It's really just the house and the money. I mean, sure, I'm stressed about messing up at work right now, but that's only because my head is so wrapped up in the foreclosure. I'm not sitting around worrying about my health or anything else like that. It's just this one big thing hanging over me.

symptom_reasoning.S056: The patient denies excessive worry across multiple life domains, stating that their anxiety is confined solely to the foreclosure and finances rather than a number of events or activities.

turns.doctor_question: Would you say that feeling anxious or on edge is the main thing you're experiencing, more so than feeling down or discouraged about your situation?
turns.patient_response: Yeah, I'd say so. I don't really feel... depressed or defeated, exactly. It's more just this constant panic. I'm always wound up tight, just waiting for the next phone call or letter from the bank to show up. So, yeah, being anxious and on edge is definitely the biggest part of it.

symptom_reasoning.S058: The patient explicitly confirms feeling constantly 'wound up tight' and 'anxious and on edge.'
symptom_reasoning.S024: The patient denies feeling depressed or defeated, stating that is not really what they are experiencing.
